fields.title: Amos
fields.subtitle: Amos, “Burden-bearer”
fields.description: The words of a herdsman from Tekoa whom the LORD sent north to the royal sanctuary at Bethel, in the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, to tell a wealthy and very religious people that God had seen what their comfort cost the poor. Crime upon crime of the nations, and then Israel’s own; “You alone have I known”; the cows of Bashan; “Prepare to meet your God”; “Seek me and live!”; the festivals God hates, and the cry “let justice roll on like water”; visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit; a famine of hearing the word of the LORD; and, at the end, the fallen booth of David raised up again. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Amos?
qa.answer: The third of the twelve shorter prophetic books of the Old Testament, and one of the earliest prophetic books to be written down. In nine chapters it pronounces judgment on Israel’s neighbours and then on Israel itself (chapters 1–2), gathers Amos’s sermons against injustice, empty worship and complacency (3–6), and records five visions, with the story of Amos’s clash with the priest of Bethel (7–9). It ends with a promise that God will raise up “the fallen booth of David” and plant his people in their land for good.

qa.question: Who was Amos, and when did he prophesy?
qa.answer: A herdsman and sheep breeder from Tekoa, a village in Judah south of Bethlehem, who also took care of sycamore-fig trees. He insisted, “I am not a prophet, nor a member of a company of prophets” (7:14): the LORD took him from the flock and sent him to the northern kingdom of Israel. The book dates his words to the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, “two years before the earthquake” (1:1), which most scholars place around 760 BC. His name probably comes from a Hebrew word for carrying a load, which is why it is often explained as “burden-bearer”.

qa.question: What does “let justice roll on like water” mean?
qa.answer: In Amos 5:24 God answers Israel’s crowded festivals and loud songs by saying that he wants something else: “let justice roll on like water, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.” In a land where most streambeds dry up in summer, it is a call for justice that never fails, for the poor and for everyone, in the courts and the markets. Martin Luther King Jr. took up the verse in his 1963 speech in Washington, and it has been quoted in the cause of justice ever since.

qa.question: Why does God reject Israel’s worship in Amos?
qa.answer: Not because worship is wrong, but because the worshippers were oppressing the poor. Amos’s hearers brought sacrifices and tithes and sang to the harp, while they sold “the needy for a pair of sandals” (2:6), took bribes in court and cheated with dishonest scales. So God says, “I hate, I despise your festivals” (5:21). The prophet himself breaks into hymns of praise, and calls the people to seek the LORD, which he defines as “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the courts” (5:15).

qa.question: What are the visions of Amos?
qa.answer: Five visions in chapters 7–9. In the first two, a swarm of locusts and a consuming fire, Amos prays “How can Jacob survive? He is so small”, and the LORD relents. In the third the Lord stands by a wall with a plumb line, the builder’s test for what is straight, and judgment is fixed. The fourth, a basket of summer fruit, rests on a pun: the Hebrew for summer fruit, qayits, sounds like qets, “end”. In the fifth Amos sees the Lord standing at the altar, commanding the shrine to be struck down.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Instead, let justice roll on like water, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.

— Amos 5:24

Amos was not a professional prophet, and he said so. He was a herdsman from Tekoa, a village in the hills of Judah south of Bethlehem, a man who bred sheep and tended sycamore-fig trees. Then the LORD took him from the flock and sent him north, across the border into the kingdom of Israel, to tell a prosperous and very religious people that God was about to bring their world to an end.

His book opens with a roar: “The LORD roars from Zion and thunders from Jerusalem; the shepherds’ pastures dry up, and the summit of Carmel withers.” A shepherd knows what a lion’s roar means. It means the lion has already found its prey.

A herdsman at the king’s sanctuary

The first verse dates Amos’s words to the reigns of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, “two years before the earthquake”. The earthquake was remembered for centuries; the prophet Zechariah still speaks of people fleeing from it. Most scholars place Amos’s preaching around 760 BC, a little before Hosea began, in the long and successful reign of Jeroboam II.

Those were good years for Israel, or seemed so. Its borders had been pushed back almost to where they had been in Solomon’s day; trade flourished; the wealthy built winter houses and summer houses, “houses of ivory”, and lay on couches eating the best lamb and drinking wine by the bowlful. The shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were crowded with worshippers and offerings. Everyone agreed that God was on their side.

But the wealth was not shared, and Amos saw who paid for it. The poor were sold into slavery for debts as small as the price of a pair of sandals; merchants cheated with false weights; the courts took bribes; the needy were pushed aside at the gate where justice was meant to be done. Amos preached at Bethel, the royal sanctuary, and the priest there, Amaziah, finally sent word to the king that “The land cannot endure all his words.”

Three crimes, even four

The book’s first two chapters are a masterpiece of preaching. Amos begins by pronouncing judgment on Israel’s neighbours, one by one, each in the same pattern: “For three crimes of Damascus, even for four, I will not hold back the punishment.” Damascus for its cruelty in war; Gaza and Tyre for selling whole communities into slavery; Edom for hunting down his brother with the sword; Ammon for ripping open pregnant women to enlarge its borders; Moab for desecrating a king’s bones.

We can imagine his audience at Bethel applauding. The circle closes on the nations around them, and then on Judah, their rival to the south. And then, without warning, it closes on them:

The LORD says this: For three crimes of Israel, even for four, I will not hold back the punishment, because they sell the innocent for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.

— Amos 2:6

The neighbours were condemned for atrocities in war. Israel is condemned for what it does to its own poor in peacetime, and it receives the longest sentence of all. The nations sinned against common decency; Israel sinned against the God who brought it out of Egypt and gave it prophets, and against the poor whom his law protected.

“You alone have I known”

Israel believed that being God’s chosen people made it safe. Amos turns that belief inside out:

You alone have I known out of all the families of the earth; that is why I will punish you for all your sins.

— Amos 3:2

To be known by God, chosen and loved by him, is not a shelter from his judgment but the reason for it. The more light a people has been given, the more is asked of it. Amos follows this with a string of questions, each about cause and effect: does a lion roar with no prey, does a trap spring with nothing in it? So too with him: “The lion has roared; who will not be afraid? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can keep from prophesying?” He preached because he could not keep silent.

“Yet you did not return to me”

Chapter 4 begins with the wealthy women of Samaria, whom Amos calls “cows of Bashan”, after the famous fat cattle of the plain east of the Jordan: they “oppress the poor and crush the needy” and tell their husbands, “Bring us something to drink!” Then it mocks the busy worship of the shrines: “Go to Bethel and rebel!”

Next comes one of the saddest passages in the prophets. God lists the warnings he has already sent, famine, drought, blight, locusts, plague, war, and after each the same refrain tolls like a bell: “Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.” Five times it sounds. And then there is nothing left but this:

So this is what I will do to you, Israel; and because I am going to do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel!

— Amos 4:12

Amos does not leave it as a threat. He follows it at once with a hymn to the God they must meet: the one “who forms the mountains and creates the wind”, who “turns the dawn into darkness”. Short hymns like this one break into the book three times (4:13; 5:8–9; 9:5–6), each crowned with his name: “the LORD is his name”. The God of justice is the maker of the stars.

“Seek me and live”

Chapter 5 opens with a funeral song, sung over a nation that still thinks itself alive: “Fallen, never to rise again, is Virgin Israel.” Yet inside the lament is an invitation, repeated three times: “Seek me and live!” “Seek the LORD and live”. “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live”. To seek God, Amos insists, is not to go on pilgrimage to Bethel or Gilgal or Beersheba. It is to “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the courts.” Even then he offers no easy promise, only a hope: “It may be that the LORD God of Armies will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”

Many in Israel longed for the day of the LORD, expecting it to be the day God would defeat their enemies. Amos tells them that it will be like a man who runs from a lion and meets a bear, then gets home, leans his hand against the wall, and is bitten by a snake:

Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD! Why do you want the day of the LORD? It will be darkness, not light.

— Amos 5:18

And then comes the most famous passage in the book. God speaks of Israel’s festivals, offerings and songs, and his words are blunt: “I hate, I despise your festivals”; “Take the noise of your songs away from me”. What he wants instead is the verse at the head of this introduction, justice rolling on like water, righteousness like a stream that never runs dry. In a land where streambeds dry up in summer, Amos asks for a justice that never fails. In 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. took up this verse in Washington, in his speech “I Have a Dream”, and it has been a watchword of the struggle for justice ever since.

At ease in Zion

Chapter 6 turns to the leaders, “the complacent in Zion” and “those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria”. They lie on beds inlaid with ivory, improvise songs to the harp, and anoint themselves with the finest oils, “but they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.” Amos’s charge is not only that they did wrong. It is that they did not care. So they will be the first to go into exile.

Five visions

The last three chapters are built around five visions. In the first two, God shows Amos a swarm of locusts and a consuming fire, and twice Amos prays, “How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” Twice the LORD relents. Amos is a prophet of judgment, but he is first an intercessor.

In the third vision the Lord stands beside a wall with a plumb line in his hand, the builder’s tool for testing whether a wall is straight. Israel has been measured, and it is crooked. This time there is no reprieve: “I will no longer pass them by.”

Here the story breaks in. Amaziah the priest of Bethel tells Amos to go home to Judah and do his prophesying there, “for it is the king’s sanctuary and a royal temple.” Amos’s answer is one of the great statements of a prophet’s calling:

Amos answered Amaziah, “I am not a prophet, nor a member of a company of prophets. I am a herdsman, and I take care of sycamore-fig trees. But the LORD took me from tending the flock and told me, ‘Go and prophesy to my people Israel.’

— Amos 7:14–15

The fourth vision is a basket of summer fruit. The point is a pun: the Hebrew for “summer fruit”, qayits, sounds like the word for “end”, qets. Israel is ripe, and “The end has come upon my people Israel.” With it comes one of the most chilling threats in Scripture, not a famine of bread but “for hearing the words of the LORD”: people will run back and forth searching for God’s word, “but they will not find it.” In the fifth vision Amos sees the Lord himself standing by the altar, commanding the shrine to be struck down. There is nowhere to hide from him, whether in Sheol, in the heavens or at the bottom of the sea.

The fallen booth of David

Then, in the book’s last verses, the light breaks through. God will shake Israel among the nations as grain is shaken in a sieve, but he will not destroy the house of Jacob completely. And after the judgment:

On that day I will raise up the fallen booth of David. I will wall up its gaps and restore its ruins and rebuild it as it was in days long ago, so that they may possess what is left of Edom and every nation that is called by my name, declares the LORD, who will do this.

— Amos 9:11–12

The book that began with withered pastures ends with mountains dripping sweet wine, ruined cities rebuilt, and a people planted in their land never to be uprooted again. Some scholars think these closing verses were added after the exile, because their tone is so different from what comes before; others answer that a prophet who prayed for Jacob could also foresee his healing, and that judgment without hope would not be the God of Amos at all. When the apostles met in Jerusalem to decide whether Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses, James quoted this promise, in a form close to the ancient Greek translation, as foretelling the very thing they were seeing: “so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, all the nations that are called by my name”.

How to read Amos

Amos is a book for reading aloud. Its patterns, the “For three crimes…, even for four”, the refrain “Yet you did not return to me”, the repeated “Seek”, are made for the ear. Read chapters 1–2 in one go to feel the trap closing; chapters 3–6 as a series of sermons, most beginning “Hear this word” or “Woe”; and chapters 7–9 as the visions, with the clash at Bethel in the middle.

As you read, notice how concrete Amos is. He names the sandals, the false weights, the garments taken in pledge, the ivory couches. Sin, for him, is never an abstraction; it has victims. And notice that the same prophet who denounces empty worship also sings the greatest hymns in the book. Amos does not want less worship. He wants worship that cannot be separated from the way we treat the poor.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Most of Amos is poetry, and this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out; the first four visions and the story of Amaziah are printed as prose.

“The LORD” and “the Lord GOD”. Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation writes “the LORD”. Amos often joins it to the word for “Lord” or “master”, and then, as in most English Bibles, it reads “the Lord GOD”. The title that older Bibles render “the LORD God of hosts” is translated “the LORD God of Armies”.

Three crimes and four. The refrain of chapters 1–2 keeps the Hebrew’s numbers, “For three crimes of Damascus, even for four”, rather than smoothing them away. It is a way of saying “crime upon crime”: the measure is full and more than full.

Amos’s trade. The first verse calls him one of “the sheep breeders of Tekoa”, and in 7:14 he says, “I am a herdsman, and I take care of sycamore-fig trees”, a kind of fig that has to be pierced to ripen.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Amos 1
fields.body_html:
The words of Amos

The words of Amos, one of the sheep breeders of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel during the reign of Uzziah king of Judah and during the reign of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
He said:
The LORD roars from Zion
and thunders from Jerusalem;
the shepherds’ pastures dry up,
and the summit of Carmel withers.

Damascus, Gaza and Tyre

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Damascus,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they threshed Gilead with iron threshing sledges.
So I will send fire on the house of Hazael,
and it will devour the fortresses of Ben-hadad.
I will break the bar of the gate of Damascus
and cut off the ruler from the Valley of Aven
and the one who holds the scepter from Beth-eden.
The people of Aram will go into exile to Kir, says the LORD.

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Gaza,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they carried off whole communities into exile and handed them over to Edom.
So I will send fire on the wall of Gaza,
and it will devour its fortresses.
I will cut off the ruler from Ashdod
and the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon.
I will turn my hand against Ekron, and the last of the Philistines will perish,
says the Lord GOD.

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Tyre,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they handed over whole communities of captives to Edom
and did not remember the treaty of brotherhood.
So I will send fire on the wall of Tyre,
and it will devour its fortresses.

Edom and Ammon

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Edom,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because he hunted down his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion;
his anger kept tearing without end,
and he held on to his fury forever.
So I will send fire on Teman,
and it will devour the fortresses of Bozrah.

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of the Ammonites,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead
to enlarge their own territory.
So I will set fire to the wall of Rabbah,
and it will devour its fortresses
amid war cries on the day of battle,
amid a storm on the day of the whirlwind.
Their king will go into exile,
he and his officials together, says the LORD.
fields.summary: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, announces that God roars from Zion and will judge Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom and Ammon for their crimes.

fields.title: Amos 2
fields.body_html:
Moab and Judah

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Moab,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because he burned the bones of Edom’s king to lime.
So I will send fire on Moab,
and it will devour the fortresses of Kerioth.
Moab will die amid the uproar,
amid war cries and the sound of the ram’s horn.
I will cut off the ruler from among its people
and kill all its officials with him, says the LORD.

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Judah,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they rejected the instruction of the LORD and did not keep his statutes;
their lies have led them astray,
the lies their ancestors followed.
So I will send fire on Judah,
and it will devour the fortresses of Jerusalem.

Israel

The LORD says this:
For three crimes of Israel,
even for four, I will not hold back the punishment,
because they sell the innocent for silver
and the needy for a pair of sandals.
They trample the heads of the poor into the dust of the ground
and push the humble out of the way.
A man and his father sleep with the same young woman,
and so they profane my holy name.
They stretch out on garments taken in pledge
beside every altar,
and they drink wine taken as fines
in the house of their God.
Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorites before them,
though they were as tall as cedars
and as strong as oaks.
I destroyed their fruit above
and their roots below.
It was I who brought you up from the land of Egypt
and led you through the wilderness for forty years,
so that you could take possession of the land of the Amorites.
I raised up prophets from among your sons
and Nazirites from among your young men.
Is this not true, people of Israel? declares the LORD.
But you made the Nazirites drink wine,
and you ordered the prophets,
“Do not prophesy.”
Look, I am going to make the ground shake beneath you,
as a cart shakes
when it is loaded with sheaves.
Even the swift will have no way to escape,
the strong will not be able to use his strength,
and the warrior will not save his own life.
The archer will not stand his ground,
the swift runner will not get away,
and the horseman will not save his life.
Even the bravest of the warriors
will flee naked on that day, declares the LORD.
fields.summary: God will judge Moab and Judah, and Israel for selling the righteous for silver and trampling the poor.

fields.title: Amos 3
fields.body_html:
You alone have I known

Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, people of Israel,
against the whole family
that I brought up from the land of Egypt:
You alone have I known
out of all the families of the earth;
that is why I will punish you
for all your sins.
Do two people walk together
unless they have agreed to meet?
Does a lion roar in the forest
when it has no prey?
Does a young lion growl from its den
unless it has caught something?
Does a bird fall into a trap on the ground
if no snare has been set for it?
Does a trap spring up from the ground
when it has caught nothing?
If a ram’s horn is blown in a city,
do the people not tremble?
If disaster comes to a city,
has the LORD not done it?
The Lord GOD does nothing at all
unless he first reveals his plan
to his servants the prophets.
The lion has roared; who will not be afraid?
The Lord GOD has spoken;
who can keep from prophesying?
Announce to the fortresses of Ashdod
and to the fortresses in the land of Egypt, and say:
“Assemble on the mountains around Samaria
and see the great turmoil within her
and the oppression in her midst.”
They do not know how to do right, declares the LORD,
these people who hoard violence and destruction in their fortresses.

An enemy will surround the land

Therefore the Lord GOD says this:
An enemy will surround the land;
he will tear down your strongholds,
and your fortresses will be plundered.
The LORD says this:
As a shepherd snatches from a lion’s mouth just two legs or a scrap of an ear,
so will the people of Israel who live in Samaria be rescued,
with nothing but the corner of a bed or a scrap of silk from a couch.
Listen, and be witnesses against Jacob’s house,
declares the Lord GOD, the God of Armies.
On the day I punish Israel for its crimes,
I will punish the altars of Bethel;
the horns of the altar will be broken off
and fall to the ground.
I will strike down the winter house together with the summer house;
the houses of ivory will be destroyed, and the great houses will be swept away, declares the LORD.
fields.summary: God chose Israel from all the families of the earth, so God will punish them for all their sins.

fields.title: Amos 4
fields.body_html:
Hear this word, cows of Bashan

Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on the hill of Samaria,
you who oppress the poor
and crush the needy,
who say to their husbands, “Bring us something to drink!”
The Lord GOD has sworn by his holiness:
The time is surely coming for you
when you will be dragged away with hooks,
the last of you with fishhooks.
You will go out through the breaches in the wall, each one straight ahead,
and you will be thrown out toward Harmon, declares the LORD.
Go to Bethel and rebel!
Go to Gilgal and rebel even more!
Bring your sacrifices every morning,
your tithes every three days!
Burn a thank offering of leavened bread,
and announce your freewill offerings, make them known!
For this is what you love to do, people of Israel,
declares the Lord GOD.
I also gave you clean teeth in all your cities
and lack of bread in all your towns.
Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.
I also held back the rain from you when the harvest was still three months away.
I would send rain on one town
but no rain on another.
One field would get rain,
and the field that got none would dry up.
People from two or three towns staggered to another town for water but could not get enough to drink.
Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.
I struck you with blight and mildew;
the cutting locust devoured your many gardens and vineyards, your fig trees and olive groves.
Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.

I sent a plague among you as I did on Egypt;
I killed your young men with the sword,
and your horses were captured;
I made the stench of your camps fill your nostrils.
Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.
I overthrew some of you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,
and you became like a burning stick pulled out of the fire.
Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD.

Prepare to meet your God

So this is what I will do to you, Israel;
and because I am going to do this to you,
prepare to meet your God, Israel!
For he is the one who forms the mountains and creates the wind, who reveals his thoughts to humankind,
who turns the dawn into darkness
and treads on the heights of the earth:
The LORD God of Armies is his name.
fields.summary: The wealthy women of Samaria oppress the poor, and Israel did not return to God despite famine, drought and plague, so they must prepare to meet their God.

fields.title: Amos 5
fields.body_html:
A lament for Israel

Hear this word, house of Israel, this lament I raise over you:
Fallen, never to rise again, is Virgin Israel;
she lies abandoned on her own land, with no one to lift her up.
For the Lord GOD says this:
The city that marches out a thousand strong will be left with a hundred,
and the one that marches out a hundred strong will be left with ten, in the house of Israel.

Seek the LORD and live

For the LORD says this to the house of Israel:
Seek me and live!
Do not seek Bethel;
do not go to Gilgal
or cross over to Beersheba.
For Gilgal is sure to go into exile,
and Bethel will be reduced to nothing.
Seek the LORD and live,
or he will sweep through the house of Joseph like fire;
it will burn, and there will be no one at Bethel to put it out.
You turn justice into bitter wormwood
and throw righteousness to the ground.
He made the Pleiades and Orion; he turns deep darkness into morning
and darkens day into night.
He calls up the waters of the sea and pours them out across the face of the earth: the LORD is his name.

He makes destruction blaze out against the strong,
and ruin comes upon the fortress.
They hate anyone who rebukes wrongdoing in court
and detest whoever speaks honestly.
Therefore, because you trample on the poor and force them to hand over their grain,
you have built houses of cut stone, but you will not live in them;
you have planted fine vineyards,
but you will not drink their wine.
For I know how many your crimes are
and how great your sins:
you oppress the innocent and take bribes,
and you push aside the poor in court.
So at such a time the prudent keep quiet,
for it is an evil time.
Seek good and not evil, so that you may live,
and so that the LORD God of Armies may truly be with you, as you claim he is.
Hate evil and love good;
establish justice in the courts.
It may be that the LORD God of Armies will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

Wailing in every street

Therefore the LORD God of Armies, the Lord, says this:
There will be wailing in every square,
and in every street people will cry, “Alas! Alas!”
They will call the farmers to mourn
and the professional mourners to wail.
There will be wailing in every vineyard,
for I will pass through the middle of you, says the LORD.

The day of the LORD

Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD!
Why do you want the day of the LORD? It will be darkness, not light.
It will be as when a man runs from a lion
and a bear meets him,
or he goes home
and leans his hand against the wall,
and a snake bites him.
Will not the day of the LORD be darkness, not light,
pitch dark, with no brightness in it?
I hate, I despise your festivals;
I take no pleasure in your sacred assemblies.
Even if you sacrifice burnt offerings and grain offerings to me, I will not accept them;
I will not look at the peace offerings of your fattened animals.
Take the noise of your songs away from me;
I will not listen to the music of your harps.
Instead, let justice roll on like water,
and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.
Was it sacrifices and offerings that you brought me during the forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
So you will carry off Sikkuth, your king,
and Kiyyun, your idols,
the star of your god,
which you made for yourselves.
So I will take you into exile beyond Damascus,
says the LORD; the God of Armies is his name.
fields.summary: Amos laments for Israel and calls the people to seek God and live, and to let justice roll on like water.

fields.title: Amos 6
fields.body_html:
Woe to those at ease in Zion

Woe to the complacent in Zion,
and to those who feel secure on the mountain of Samaria,
the notable leaders of the foremost nation,
to whom the house of Israel comes!
Go over to Calneh and look;
go on from there to Hamath the great,
then go down to Philistine Gath. Are those cities better than your kingdoms?
Is their land larger than yours?
You put off the day of disaster,
yet you bring near the reign of violence.
They lie on beds inlaid with ivory
and sprawl on their couches;
they eat lambs from the flock
and calves fattened in the stall.
They improvise songs to the sound of the harp,
and like David they invent musical instruments for themselves.
They drink wine by the bowlful
and anoint themselves with the finest oils,
but they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.
So now they will be the first to go into exile,
and the feasting of the loungers will come to an end.

The proud city handed over

The Lord GOD has sworn by himself, declares the LORD God of Armies:
I detest the pride of Jacob
and hate his fortresses;
I will hand over the city and everything in it.
If ten people are left in one house, they too will die.
When a relative who is to burn the dead comes to carry the bodies out of the house,
he will call to someone hiding deep inside the house, “Is anyone else with you?” When the answer comes, “No,”
he will say, “Hush!
We must not mention the name of the LORD.”
For look, the LORD gives the command,
and the great house will be broken into fragments,
and the small house into splinters.
Do horses gallop over rocky crags?
Does anyone plow rock with oxen?
Yet you have made justice into poison
and the fruit of righteousness into bitter wormwood.
You rejoice over Lo-debar
and say, “Did we not capture Karnaim
with our own strength?”
For look, I am about to raise up a nation against you, house of Israel, declares the LORD God of Armies,
and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of the Arabah.
fields.summary: Woe to those at ease in Zion who lie on beds of ivory but do not grieve over Israel’s ruin.

fields.title: Amos 7
fields.body_html:
Locusts and fire

This is what the Lord GOD showed me: he was forming swarms of locusts just as the late crop was beginning to come up, the crop that grows after the king’s share has been mown. When they had eaten up the green plants of the land, I said, “Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” So the LORD relented. “It will not happen,” the LORD said. This is what the Lord GOD showed me: there was the Lord GOD, summoning fire to judge. It dried up the great deep and was eating up the land. Then I said, “Lord GOD, please stop! How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” So the LORD relented. “This will not happen either,” the Lord GOD said.

The plumb line

This is what he showed me: the Lord was standing beside a wall built true to a plumb line, with a plumb line in his hand. The LORD asked me, “What do you see, Amos?” I answered, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord said, “Look, I am placing a plumb line among my people Israel. I will no longer pass them by. Isaac’s high places will be made desolate and Israel’s sanctuaries will lie in ruins, and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”

Amos and Amaziah

Amaziah the priest of Bethel then sent a message to Jeroboam king of Israel: “Amos is plotting against you in the very heart of Israel. The land cannot endure all his words. For this is what Amos is saying: ‘Jeroboam is going to die by the sword, and Israel will certainly be exiled, away from its land.’”

Then Amaziah said to Amos, “Go away, you seer! Run off to the land of Judah. Make your living there, and do your prophesying there. But never prophesy again at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and a royal temple.”

Amos answered Amaziah, “I am not a prophet, nor a member of a company of prophets. I am a herdsman, and I take care of sycamore-fig trees. But the LORD took me from tending the flock and told me, ‘Go and prophesy to my people Israel.’ So now hear the word of the LORD. You tell me, ‘Do not prophesy against Israel, and stop preaching against the house of Isaac.’ Therefore the LORD says this: ‘Your wife will be made a prostitute in the city, your sons and daughters will be struck down by the sword, and your land will be measured out and divided. You yourself will die in an unclean land, and Israel will surely go into exile, away from its land.’”
fields.summary: Amos sees visions of locusts, fire and a plumb line. Amaziah the priest tells Amos to go back to Judah, and Amos answers that God called him.

fields.title: Amos 8
fields.body_html:
A basket of summer fruit

This is what the Lord GOD showed me: a basket of summer fruit. He asked, “What do you see, Amos?” I answered, “A basket of summer fruit.” Then the LORD said to me, “The end has come upon my people Israel. Never again will I pass them by. On that day the songs of the temple will turn to wailing, declares the Lord GOD. There will be many dead bodies, thrown out everywhere. Hush!”

Cheating the poor

Hear this,
you who trample on the needy
and would wipe out the poor of the land,
who say, “When will the new moon festival be over, so that we can sell grain?
When will the sabbath end, so that we can put out wheat for sale,
making the ephah smaller and the shekel heavier,
and cheating with dishonest scales,
so that we can purchase the poor with silver
and the needy for the price of a pair of sandals,
and even sell the sweepings with the wheat?”
The LORD has sworn by the pride of Jacob:
Never will I forget anything they have done.
Will not the land shake because of this,
and all who live in it mourn?
All of it will rise like the Nile;
it will heave and sink again like the Nile of Egypt.

Darkness at noon and a famine of the word

On that day, declares the Lord GOD,
I will make the sun set at noon
and darken the earth in broad daylight.
I will turn your festivals into mourning and all your songs into laments;
I will put sackcloth around every waist
and make every head bald.
I will make that time like mourning for an only son,
and its end a bitter day.
The days are coming, declares the Lord GOD,
when I am going to send famine through the land:
not hunger for bread or thirst for water,
but for hearing the words of the LORD.
People will stagger from sea to sea
and wander from north to east;
they will run back and forth, searching for the word of the LORD, but they will not find it.
On that day the beautiful young women and the young men will faint from thirst.
Those who swear by Samaria’s guilt
and say, “As surely as your god lives, Dan,”
or, “As surely as the way of Beersheba lives,”
will fall and never rise again.
fields.summary: A basket of summer fruit means the end has come for Israel. A famine is coming, not of bread, but of hearing the words of God.

fields.title: Amos 9
fields.body_html:
The Lord beside the altar

I saw the Lord standing at the altar, and he said: Strike the pillar tops until the thresholds shake, and bring them down on the heads of all the people;
those who are left I will kill with the sword.
Not one of them will get away;
not one will escape alive.
Though they dig down into Sheol,
my hand will take them from there;
though they climb up to the heavens,
from there I will bring them down.
Though they hide on the top of Carmel,
I will search them out and take them from there;
though they hide from my sight on the floor of the sea,
there I will order the serpent to bite them.
Though they go into captivity, driven ahead of their enemies,
there I will command the sword to kill them.
I will fix my eyes on them for harm and not for good.
The Lord GOD of Armies touches the earth and it melts,
and all who live in it mourn;
all of it rises like the Nile
and sinks again like the Nile of Egypt.
He builds his upper chambers in the heavens
and sets his vault firmly over the earth.
He calls up the waters of the sea and pours them out across the face of the earth: the LORD is his name.
Are you not like the Cushites to me, people of Israel? declares the LORD.
Did I not bring Israel up out of Egypt,
and the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir?
Look, the Lord GOD’s eyes are on the sinful kingdom,
and I will wipe it off the face of the earth.
Yet I will not destroy the house of Jacob completely, declares the LORD.
For look, I am about to give the command:
I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations
the way grain is shaken in a sieve,
and not a pebble will fall to the ground.
All the sinners among my people will die by the sword,
those who say, “Disaster will not overtake us or come upon us.”
On that day
I will raise up the fallen booth of David.
I will wall up its gaps and restore its ruins
and rebuild it as it was in days long ago,
so that they may possess what is left of Edom
and every nation that is called by my name,
declares the LORD, who will do this.

The days are coming

The days are coming, declares the LORD,
when the one who plows will catch up with the one who reaps,
and the one who treads grapes with the one who sows the seed.
The mountains will drip with sweet wine,
and all the hills will flow with it.
I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel.
They will rebuild the ruined cities and live in them;
they will plant vineyards and drink the wine from them;
they will lay out gardens and eat their fruit.
I will plant them in their own land,
and they will never again be pulled up from the land I have given them,
says the LORD your God.
fields.summary: God stands by the altar and no one can escape judgment. Yet God will raise up David’s fallen shelter and restore the fortunes of Israel.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
I will plant them in their own land, and they will never again be pulled up from the land I have given them, says the LORD your God.

— Amos 9:15

Amos ends with a promise of roots. A herdsman who spent his life among growing things, figs and flocks and pastures, closes his book with God as a farmer planting his people in their land so deeply that nothing will pull them up again. It is a surprising last word from the sternest of the prophets, and it changes how the rest of the book sounds.

The question the book leaves with you

Amos asks what God sees when he looks at our worship. Israel’s festivals were crowded and its songs were loud, and God would not listen to them, because the same people who sang in the sanctuary sold the needy for a pair of sandals on the way home. Amos will not let us separate the two. He asks whether our religion has anything to do with the courts, the markets, the wages, the weights and measures, the people at the gate who have no one to speak for them.

And he asks whether we are at ease. His harshest words are kept not for open unbelievers but for the comfortable, for those who “do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph”. The opposite of the complacency he condemns is not frantic activity but grief, the kind that moved Amos himself to pray, “How can Jacob survive? He is so small.”

Where the story goes next

Within forty years of Amos’s preaching, the northern kingdom was gone. The Assyrians took Samaria in 722 BC, and the people Amos warned were carried into exile “beyond Damascus”, as he had said. The shrine at Bethel was later torn down by King Josiah of Judah.

But the promise of “the fallen booth of David” did not fall with it. The New Testament hears it kept in Jesus, the son of David, and in the church gathered from every nation. When James quoted it at the council in Jerusalem, he was explaining why Gentiles who turned to God did not have to become Jews first: the rebuilt house of David was always meant to have room for the nations.

Where to go from here

  • On walking with God (Amos 3:3). A. W. Tozer’s sermon How to Cultivate the Holy Spirit’s Companionship, which takes as its text Amos’s question, “Do two people walk together unless they have agreed to meet?”, and asks what it means to be agreed with God.
  • On God revealing his plans to the prophets (Amos 3:7). The chapter “The Prophets: The Revelation of God’s Secrets” in Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, which takes its title from this verse and traces the promises of restoration through all the prophets, Amos 9 among them.
  • On the sieve (Amos 9:9). Charles H. Spurgeon’s reading for June 20 in Morning by Morning, and his reading for September 23 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, which read the verse, as the King James Version renders it, as a promise that not the least grain will be lost.
  • On Amos and the gospel. Augustine’s The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 28, on what Hosea and Amos foretold of Christ; and Jerome’s letter to Paulinus (Letter LIII in The Letters of St. Jerome), with its brief, vivid summary of the herdsman’s visions, from the plumb line to the famine of the word.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Amos in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read the book again, and listen for the invitation inside the warnings. The God who roars from Zion is the God who says, three times over, that he would rather his people lived:

Seek good and not evil, so that you may live, and so that the LORD God of Armies may truly be with you, as you claim he is.

— Amos 5:14
